content: The document focuses on breastfeeding practices in the context of Zika virus transmission and their implementation. It is part of a broader effort to evaluate evidence for potential medical reasons that might justify a mother temporarily or permanently ceasing breastfeeding. This guideline is linked to other emergency guidelines addressing care for pregnant women with Zika virus infection, management of microcephaly, and Guillain–Barré syndrome in the context of Zika virus outbreaks. The primary audience includes governments, health ministries, policymakers, and healthcare workers in regions affected by Zika virus transmission. It may also serve as a resource for public communication. Zika virus is an arbovirus belonging to the Flavivirus genus. Symptoms of Zika virus infection are typically mild and include fever, skin rashes, conjunctivitis, muscle and joint pain, malaise, and headache, lasting 2–7 days. The virus was first identified in sentinel Rhesus monkeys in Uganda's Zika forest in 1948 and later isolated from Aedes africanus mosquitoes in the same forest. Since then, Zika virus infections have been reported in several African countries, including the Central African Republic, Côte d’Ivoire, Gabon, Nigeria, Sierra Leone, and Uganda. It has also been identified in Asia and the Pacific, including Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, Pakistan, and Yap Island in Micronesia. The first epidemic was reported in Yap Island in 2007, with 49 confirmed cases. Subsequent outbreaks occurred in French Polynesia in 2013, the Americas (Brazil and Colombia), and Africa (Cabo Verde) in 2015. In Brazil, a clustering of fever and rash cases was detected in February 2015, confirmed as Zika virus in May 2015. By December 2015, over 50,000 suspected cases were reported in 29 Brazilian states. By March 2016, suspected Zika infections in Brazil were estimated between 500,000 and 1,500,000, with nearly 60,000 cases in Colombia and 8,000 in Cabo Verde. As of May 2016, 60 countries and territories reported ongoing mosquito-borne Zika virus transmission, with 46 experiencing their first outbreak since 2015. On February 1, 2016, the World Health Organization (WHO) declared the Zika virus outbreak and associated microcephaly and Guillain–Barré syndrome a Public Health Emergency of International Concern. Zika virus is primarily transmitted to humans through the bite of infected Aedes mosquitoes. However, person-to-person transmission has been reported via sexual contact, blood transfusion, and perinatal transmission. While mosquito bites remain the main mode of transmission, the widespread nature of the virus has raised questions about potential transmission through breastfeeding, a critical practice for infant survival and development. This publication is a WHO guideline, which provides recommendations on health interventions, including clinical, public health, or policy measures. These recommendations guide policymakers, healthcare providers, and patients in making informed decisions. The guideline has been approved by the WHO Guidelines Review Committee. The interim guidance on breastfeeding in the context of Zika virus, published by WHO, was developed through expert consensus during a teleconference on February 19, 2016. The discussions identified areas with limited evidence, recommended further research, and emphasized the need for a systematic review of evidence. This guideline replaces the interim guidance and contributes to updating evidence on acceptable medical reasons for using breast-milk substitutes, serving as a tool for health professionals and as part of the Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative package. A systematic review, registered in PROSPERO, aimed to assess the presence of Zika virus and Zika-specific antibodies in breast milk and other breastfeeding-related bodily fluids. The review included studies involving lactating women with suspected, probable, or confirmed Zika virus infection, as well as infants and young children consuming breast milk from infected mothers. Critical outcomes included the incidence of Zika virus infection in breastfeeding infants and the presence and viability of the virus in breast milk, serum, sweat, or saliva of lactating women. The search, conducted on March 14, 2016, included multiple electronic databases and ongoing or unpublished studies. Observational studies, case studies, and surveillance reports were reviewed, identifying 472 records, of which 42 were assessed for eligibility. Only three mother–infant pairs with confirmed Zika virus infection were found, all symptomatic within three days of delivery. Two infants had confirmed Zika virus infection, and the virus was detected in the breast milk of all three mothers. However, the data were insufficient to conclude transmission via breastfeeding. The guideline recommends that infants born to mothers with suspected, probable, or confirmed Zika virus infection, or residing in areas of ongoing transmission, should be fed according to normal infant feeding guidelines. Breastfeeding should begin within one hour of birth, continue exclusively for six months, and be complemented with safe, adequate foods while breastfeeding continues up to two years or beyond. This strong recommendation reflects confidence that the benefits of breastfeeding outweigh potential risks in the context of Zika virus transmission. The guideline development group considered the significant benefits of breastfeeding for mothers and children, including reduced infectious morbidity and mortality, improved intelligence, and prevention of breast cancer. While Zika virus RNA has been detected in breast milk, no documented cases of transmission through breastfeeding exist. The frequency, kinetics, and viral load of Zika virus in breast milk remain unknown. No long-term complications have been reported in infants with confirmed Zika virus infection. However, ongoing monitoring is essential, particularly in countries with active Zika virus transmission.
